q: Why does a bank’s ability to manage risk matter to investors?
options: Risk management has no effect on a bank’s profits
Even a bank with large revenues can see profits fall if loan losses are not controlled
Value investors prefer banks that take excessive risks
Governments forbid investment in banks that manage risk
explain: Weak risk management leads to losses on loans, which lowers profits despite high revenue. Value investors favour banks that earn profits without excessive risk of losing money.

q: Besides events in the economy or financial markets, banking risks can also arise from
options: staff oversight or mala fide intention that erodes asset values
only changes in the repo rate
explain: Mistakes or dishonest intent of staff can erode the value of assets and reduce the bank’s intrinsic value.

q: Which of the following is NOT a component of a bank’s risk management system?
options: Internal process of capital adequacy assessment
Fixing the repo rate for the economy
explain: The repo rate is set by the RBI’s monetary policy. A bank’s risk system consists of strategy, organisation, process, internal controls, information system and capital assessment.

q: Risk management strategy and policies of a bank must include procedures for
explain: Policies are paired with procedures to identify and measure risk, that is, for risk assessment and risk management.

q: The risk that a bank cannot meet its due liabilities because current sources of funding are withdrawn is called
explain: Inability to meet due liabilities on time, caused by withdrawal of funding or inability to raise new funds, is liquidity risk.

q: Funding liquidity risk refers to
options: a loss caused by changes in exchange rates
the inability to raise new funds when existing sources of funding are withdrawn
a loss because a debtor defaults
the loss of public trust after a scam
explain: Funding liquidity risk is the inability to raise fresh funds when current funding sources dry up.

q: Market liquidity risk arises when
options: a borrower fails to repay a loan
a bank breaks anti-money laundering rules
market disruption makes it hard to convert property into liquid assets
explain: In market liquidity risk, assets cannot be turned into cash easily because of disruption in the market.

q: When rising NPAs make banks afraid of giving loans, the flow of money in the market falls. This results in
options: a fall in the bank’s NPAs
explain: With banks lending less, less cash circulates and liquidity falls; genuine customers may then fail to get loans.

q: Liquidity risk of a bank is a consequence of
options: a fall in the cost of funds
large credit loss and business loss on investments
explain: Big credit losses and losses on the bank’s investments weaken cash inflow and lead to liquidity risk.

q: The risk of adverse effects on a bank’s financial result and capital because a debtor defaults on its obligations is
explain: A debtor’s failure to meet its obligations to the bank is credit risk.

q: Which risk arises when credit risk mitigation techniques turn out less efficient than expected?
explain: Residual risk is the loss that remains because safeguards such as collateral work less well than expected.

q: A fall in the value of purchased receivables because of cash or non-cash liabilities of the former creditor to the borrower is called
explain: This is dilution risk: the purchased receivable is worth less because of the seller’s own liabilities towards the borrower.

q: Unsettled transactions, or a counterparty’s failure to deliver in a free-delivery transaction on the due date, create
explain: Failure to settle or deliver on the due date is settlement or delivery risk.

q: A counterparty failing to settle its liabilities in a transaction before the final settlement of cash flows is known as
explain: Counterparty credit risk is the risk that the other side of a transaction fails to settle before final settlement.

q: Which of the following is NOT a component of market risk?
explain: Market risk covers forex, price risk on debt and equity securities, and commodity risk. Legal risk belongs to the operational family.

q: The risk of adverse effects on banking book items because of changes in interest rates is called
explain: Interest rate risk relates to the effect of interest-rate changes on the bank’s banking book items, financial result and capital.

q: Currency risk, the risk of loss from fluctuating foreign exchange rates, is sometimes referred to as
explain: Currency risk and exchange-rate risk mean the same thing: potential loss from foreign exchange movements.

q: A bank holding assets in US dollars suffers a loss when the dollar weakens against the rupee. Which risk is this?
explain: Losses caused by changes in foreign exchange rates are foreign exchange risk, which is part of market risk.

q: Risk that arises from a bank’s exposure to the same or similar source of risk, or the same or similar type of risk, is
explain: Concentration risk comes from too much exposure to one source or type of risk.

q: Bank exposure risk comprises the risks of the bank’s exposure towards
options: a single person or a group of related persons
explain: Exposure risk is about concentration of lending or exposure to one person or a group of related persons.

q: The risks of a bank’s investments in non-financial sector entities, fixed assets and investment property are called
explain: Investment risk relates to investments outside the financial sector and in fixed assets and investment property.

q: A bank cannot collect receivables from a borrower because of political, economic or social conditions in the borrower’s country. This is
explain: Country risk concerns the borrower’s country of origin and conditions there that block repayment.

q: Omissions in employees’ work, inadequate internal procedures, system failures and unforeseeable external events cause
explain: These are the sources of operational risk, which also includes legal risk.

q: Which of the following risks is included within operational risk?
explain: Operational risk is defined to include legal risk. The others belong to market, exposure or credit families.

q: The risk of loss from penalties and sanctions arising out of court disputes over breach of contractual and legal obligations is called
explain: Legal risk covers penalties and sanctions from court disputes and sanctions pronounced by a regulatory body.

q: Failure to follow laws, standards, and anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing procedures exposes a bank mainly to
explain: Compliance risk is the possibility of loss due to failure to comply with laws and procedures, including sanctions, financial losses and reputational damage.

q: Possible losses due to adverse effects on a bank’s market positioning are called
explain: Reputational risk relates to damage to the bank’s image and positioning in the market.

q: A bank loses public trust after a big fraud or scam and cannot control its operational risk. The resulting risk is mainly
explain: Negative public opinion after fraud leads to unpaid loans, large debt and rising NPAs, damaging the bank’s reputation.

q: Absence of appropriate policies and strategies, their poor implementation, or failure to respond to environmental changes leads to
explain: This is strategic risk: the bank’s strategy or response to change is inadequate.

q: As per the chapter, credit loss plus business loss results in
explain: Combined credit loss and business loss damages the bank’s reputation.

q: Which Act was framed specially to help banks recover bad loans and deal with non-performing assets?
explain: The SARFAESI Act lets banks enforce security and recover NPAs without going through lengthy court processes.

q: Where is the headquarters of SIDBI located?
explain: SIDBI, the Small Industries Development Bank of India, is headquartered at Lucknow.

q: Banking and financial services in India are regulated by which authority?
explain: The RBI is the monetary authority that regulates banking in India; SEBI handles securities and IRDA handles insurance.

q: Which of the following is a sign of stressed assets?
explain: Bounced cheques, stock shortages and deterioration in asset quality indicate stress in a loan account.

q: Assets that get an extended repayment period at a reduced interest rate are called
explain: Loans whose terms are eased with longer tenure and lower interest are restructured assets.

q: Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR) is the ratio of a bank’s capital to its
explain: CAR compares capital with risk-weighted assets and shows the bank’s cushion against losses.

q: Which of the following is NOT part of Tier-I capital?
explain: Subordinated debt forms part of Tier-II capital. Paid-up capital and reserves are Tier-I.

q: Subordinated debt forms part of which capital of a bank?
explain: Subordinated debt is supplementary capital counted in Tier-II.

q: Risk-weighted assets are calculated by considering credit risk, market risk and which other risk?
explain: Risk-weighted assets take account of credit, market and operational risk.

q: As per the 2024-25 syllabus, the minimum CAR scheduled commercial banks in India are required to maintain is
explain: The figure given in the syllabus is 9%; regulatory norms can be revised by the RBI.

q: Which of the following creates a need for a higher level of capital adequacy for banks?
options: A rise in the number of ATMs
A fall in the repo rate
explain: Basel III capital norms require banks to hold more and better quality capital.
